data.text: Every Goal Starts With a Search

data.body: • Every goal an AI pursues, from navigating a map to playing chess, is a search problem.
• The solution is always a path through a space of possibilities.
Every search has an origin and a destination.
The AI's job is finding a sequence of steps that moves from one to the other.
The complete set of all possible configurations the agent can be in.
A chess game has more states than atoms in the observable universe.
From any state, specific actions lead to new states.
The AI must know what moves are legal from wherever it currently stands.
Not all paths to the goal are equal.
Cost could be distance, time, or money — the AI minimises whichever metric you define as important.

data.text: Search problems provide a structured way to model decision-making, where the goal is to find a sequence of actions that leads from an initial state to a goal state.

data.body: BFS and DFS are the two fundamental strategies for exploring a state space.
The only difference is which states you choose to explore next.
BFS explores all states at the current depth before going deeper — like ripples spreading across water.
It uses a queue (FIFO) and guarantees the shortest path.
DFS follows one path all the way before backtracking — like a spelunker exploring one tunnel completely.
It uses a stack (LIFO) and uses far less memory than BFS.
The frontier is the set of discovered-but-unexplored states.
BFS adds to the back of a queue; DFS adds to the top of a stack.
This one difference produces completely different search orders.
BFS always finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs.
DFS finds a solution — but not necessarily the best one.
Both are complete on finite graphs.
BFS uses a queue (FIFO) to manage the frontier — first discovered, first explored.
It expands all states at the current depth before moving one level deeper.
BFS guarantees finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs — it is optimal.

items: Initialize Queue — Place the start state in a FIFO queue as your frontier.
Dequeue Front — Remove the front node — this is the current state to explore.
Check Goal — If this state is the goal, reconstruct and return the path.

data.body: The trade-off is memory: BFS can store exponentially more states than DFS.
BFS is complete — it will always find a solution if one exists on a finite graph.

items: Expand Neighbors — Add all unexplored neighbors to the back of the queue.
Repeat — Keep dequeuing from the front until the queue is empty or the goal is found.

data.body: DFS uses a stack (LIFO) — the last state discovered is always the next to explore.
It follows one path all the way to a leaf before backtracking to try another.
DFS uses dramatically less memory than BFS — only one path is stored at a time.

items: Initialize Stack — Place the start state on a LIFO stack as your frontier.
Pop Top — Pop the top node — this is the current state to explore.
Check Goal — If this state is the goal, reconstruct and return the path.

data.body: The trade-off is optimality: DFS may find a solution, but not the shortest one.
DFS is also complete on finite graphs, but it can get lost in infinite branches without depth limits.

items: Expand Neighbors — Push all unexplored neighbors onto the top of the stack.
Backtrack — When a node has no unexplored neighbors, pop the next from the stack.

data.text: BFS finds the shortest path. DFS uses the least memory. The right choice depends on what matters.

data.body: Greedy Best-First Search uses only h(n) to race toward the goal.
A* combines h(n) with g(n) to guarantee an optimal path.
A heuristic is an estimate of the remaining cost from any state to the goal.
It's a hint — not exact — but it dramatically reduces the number of states you need to explore.
Greedy search always picks the state with the lowest h(n).
It's fast but can follow misleading heuristics into dead ends, missing the optimal path.
A* combines actual cost so far g(n) with the estimated remaining cost h(n).
This balance makes it both optimal and efficient — the gold standard of search algorithms.
A heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates the true remaining cost.
Admissible heuristics guarantee that A* will always find the optimal solution.
Greedy Best-First Search always expands the state closest to the goal, using only h(n).
It picks the brightest light on the horizon — ignoring the path behind it.
The frontier is a priority queue sorted by h(n); lowest gets expanded first.
This makes it fast, but it can chase a misleading heuristic into a dead end.
Greedy is fast and dramatic — but it does not guarantee the shortest path.

items: Initialize: Place the start state in the frontier, sorted by h(n).
Expand: Pop the state with the lowest h(n) — the one that looks closest to the goal.
Goal Check: If the expanded state is the goal, return the solution.
Explore Neighbors: Add each unvisited neighbor to the frontier, scored by its h(n).
Repeat: Continue expanding the lowest-h(n) state until the goal is found or the frontier is empty.

data.body: A* combines the actual cost g(n) with the estimated remaining cost h(n).
It expands the state with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n) — balancing past and future.
This prevents A* from being tricked by a tempting but costly detour.
With an admissible heuristic (never overestimates), A* is guaranteed optimal.
A* is the gold standard of informed search — optimal, efficient, and widely used.

items: Initialize: Place the start state in the frontier with g=0, f = h(start).
Expand: Pop the state with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n).
Goal Check: If the expanded state is the goal, return the optimal solution.
Explore Neighbors: For each neighbor, compute tentative g = current.g + step_cost; add to frontier if it is an improvement.
Repeat: Continue expanding the lowest-f(n) state until the goal is found or the frontier is empty.

data.text: A* is optimal because it combines known path cost with a heuristic that never overestimates the remaining distance.

blocks.subtitle: A delivery rider needs to reach the customer across town.|Greedy takes the road that looks closest. A* checks distance and traffic ahead.

panels.description: A* avoids the traps Greedy fell for. It reaches the goal efficiently.|Always the best overall route — not just the fastest-looking one.
panels.caption: A* delivers. Greedy? Still stuck in traffic.

blocks.insight: Greedy is fast but blind — it ignores the cost of getting there.|A* sees the full picture, so it always finds the best route.
blocks.reinforcement: Greedy: "That looks closest."|A*: "That is the smartest overall route."

data.body: When your environment is actively trying to defeat you, regular search fails. Adversarial search is how AI plays games — anticipating the opponent's best moves and choosing the path that guarantees the best worst-case outcome.
Adversarial search problems are modeled as game trees where players take alternating turns, with each node representing a game state.
The minimax algorithm recursively evaluates game states, assuming both players play optimally to minimize the maximum possible loss.
Alpha-beta pruning optimizes minimax by pruning branches that cannot affect the final decision, dramatically reducing the search space.
In normal search (like A*), the AI just needs to find a path to the goal. The environment is static.
In adversarial search (like Chess or Tic-Tac-Toe), there is an opponent who is actively trying to stop the AI from winning.
We assume the opponent is perfectly rational and will always make the move that is worst for us.
Therefore, we can't just pick a path that looks good — we have to pick the path that survives the opponent's best counter-attacks.

items: Static Search — In normal search (like A*), the AI just needs to find a path to the goal. The environment is static.
Adversarial Search — In adversarial search (like Chess or Tic-Tac-Toe), there is an opponent who is actively trying to stop the AI from winning.
Rational Opponent — We assume the opponent is perfectly rational and will always make the move that is worst for us.

data.body: Minimax is the foundational algorithm for two-player, zero-sum games.
We call the AI "MAX" (trying to maximize the score) and the opponent "MIN" (trying to minimize the score).
The algorithm generates the entire game tree down to the terminal states (win/loss/draw), scores them, and propagates those scores back up the tree.

items: MAX — We call the AI "MAX" (trying to maximize the score) and the opponent "MIN" (trying to minimize the score).
MIN — We call the AI "MAX" (trying to maximize the score) and the opponent "MIN" (trying to minimize the score).
Game Tree — The algorithm generates the entire game tree down to the terminal states (win/loss/draw), scores them, and propagates those scores back up the tree.

data.body: Minimax is perfect, but exploring every possible game state is impossible for complex games.
Chess has more possible games than there are atoms in the universe (10^120).
Alpha-Beta Pruning is an optimization technique for Minimax.
It keeps track of the best options found so far (Alpha for MAX, Beta for MIN) and stops evaluating a branch as soon as it proves to be worse than a previously examined branch.
This cuts the search space in half, allowing the AI to look twice as far ahead in the same amount of time, without changing the final decision.

items: Alpha — It keeps track of the best options found so far (Alpha for MAX, Beta for MIN) and stops evaluating a branch as soon as it proves to be worse than a previously examined branch.
Beta — It keeps track of the best options found so far (Alpha for MAX, Beta for MIN) and stops evaluating a branch as soon as it proves to be worse than a previously examined branch.

data.body: Even with Alpha-Beta Pruning, we still can't reach terminal states in games like Chess.
Depth-Limited search stops the algorithm after a certain number of moves (depth).
Instead of a terminal Utility function, it uses a Heuristic Evaluation Function to estimate how good the board looks at the cutoff depth.
If the AI can look 10 moves deep, it evaluates the board there, and then propagates those estimates back up.

items: Depth-Limited Search — Depth-Limited search stops the algorithm after a certain number of moves (depth).
Heuristic Evaluation Function — Instead of a terminal Utility function, it uses a Heuristic Evaluation Function to estimate how good the board looks at the cutoff depth.
Cutoff Depth — If the AI can look 10 moves deep, it evaluates the board there, and then propagates those estimates back up.

data.text: Minimax finds the optimal move by assuming the opponent will always play perfectly to minimize your score.

panels.description: X is MAX. O is MIN.

panels.label: Result

panels.label: Terminal Test
panels.description: Returns true if there's 3-in-a-row or the board is full.

panels.label: Utility Function
panels.description: Returns +1 if X wins, -1 if O wins, 0 if draw.

blocks.insight: By defining these 6 functions, Minimax can solve the game without needing any specific "strategy" hardcoded into it.
blocks.reinforcement: The AI doesn't know what "winning" feels like. It just mathematically maximizes the Utility number.

keyTakeaways.text: A search problem has a start state, goal state, actions, and path cost
BFS explores level by level — guarantees the shortest path
DFS goes deep first — uses less memory, not guaranteed optimal
The frontier is the set of discovered-but-unexplored states
A* = g(n) + h(n) — optimal when the heuristic is admissible
Admissibility means the heuristic never overestimates remaining cost

The difference between BFS and DFS — memory vs optimality
How heuristics make search dramatically faster
